mcqs.question: Why does an LRU cache's internal list use a doubly linked list rather than a singly linked one?
options: Removing a node you already hold a reference to needs its predecessor, which only a doubly linked list gives you in O(1)
Doubly linked lists support random access by index in O(1)
Singly linked lists cannot represent an ordering at all
Doubly linked lists use less memory per node
mcqs.explanation: An LRU cache needs to unlink an arbitrary node the moment it's touched, and unlinking requires updating the previous node's `next` — without a `prev` pointer you'd have to walk from the head to find it, costing O(n). Doubly linked lists cost more memory, not less, and neither variant gives O(1) indexed access.

mcqs.question: What problem does a dummy (sentinel) head node solve?
options: It makes traversal run in O(log n) instead of O(n)
It removes the need for a special-case branch when the operation targets the first real node
It converts a singly linked list into a doubly linked list
It lets you binary search the list
mcqs.explanation: Without a sentinel, deleting or inserting at the head has no predecessor to update, forcing a separate code path. Prepending a dummy node gives every real node a predecessor, so head operations use the exact same logic as any other position. It has nothing to do with traversal speed, pointer direction, or search.

mcqs.question: You're given only a reference to a node (not the head) and asked to delete it in O(1). What must be true for the standard "copy next node's value forward" trick to work?
options: The list must be circular
The node must be the head of the list
The node must not be the last node in the list
The list must be doubly linked
mcqs.explanation: The trick copies the next node's value into the given node, then unlinks the next node — which only works if a next node exists. If the given node is the tail, there is nothing to copy forward, and the operation is impossible without walking from the head. It works fine on singly linked, non-circular lists.

mcqs.question: Why must you save `node.next` into a local variable before overwriting `node.next` during a pointer-rewiring operation?
options: Local variables are faster to access than struct fields
It's required to make the list circular
It prevents the garbage collector from freeing the node early
Overwriting the field discards the old pointer, so any later step that needs the original destination loses it permanently
mcqs.explanation: Once `node.next` is reassigned, the previous value is gone — there's no way to recover it. Any subsequent step of the algorithm (reversal, splicing, insertion) that still needs the old destination must have captured it beforehand. This is about correctness of the rewiring sequence, not performance, circularity, or memory management.

mcqs.question: Two structures both support O(n) full traversal, but a linked-list traversal consistently runs several times slower than an array traversal of the same size in practice. Why?
options: Big-O notation is wrong for linked lists
Arrays always have fewer elements than linked lists
Linked list nodes are typically scattered across memory, so each `next` hop can be a cache miss, unlike an array's sequential, prefetchable layout
Linked lists require recursion, which is inherently slower than loops
mcqs.explanation: Big-O deliberately ignores memory-access cost, and that's exactly where the two structures diverge: array elements sit in a contiguous, prefetch-friendly block, while list nodes can be scattered anywhere the allocator put them, turning traversal into a chain of potential cache misses. Traversal doesn't require recursion, and array size isn't inherently smaller.

mcqs.question: A problem needs frequent inserts and deletes in the middle of a growing sequence, given a reference to the position, and never needs to look up the kth element by index. Which structure fits better?
options: A dynamic array, because it always outperforms a linked list
Neither — this requires a hash map
A linked list, because mid-sequence insert/delete at a known node is O(1) versus an array's O(n) shift
A dynamic array, because it has lower memory overhead per element
mcqs.explanation: The access pattern described — frequent structural changes at known positions, no indexed lookup — is exactly what a linked list is built for; an array would pay O(n) to shift elements on every insert/delete. Lower memory overhead is real but irrelevant when it forces O(n) operations on the hot path, and a hash map doesn't preserve sequence order.
